splits.legalQuestion: Whether a multiemployer pension plan actuary may select actuarial assumptions for calculating withdrawal liability after the statutory measurement date (the end of the prior plan year), or whether all such assumptions must be fixed by that date.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on the timing requirement for actuarial assumptions used in calculating employer withdrawal liability from multiemployer pension plans. This affects billions of dollars in potential obligations because the timing directly controls how much withdrawing employers must pay.

positions.label: Assumptions must be fixed by measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that all actuarial assumptions for calculating withdrawal liability must be selected by the statutory measurement date (end of the prior plan year), providing employers with greater predictability.

positions.label: Assumptions may be selected after measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that a plan actuary may select actuarial assumptions after the statutory measurement date, allowing use of more current data in calculating withdrawal liability.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the term of supervised release is tolled (paused) when a supervisee absconds from supervision, thereby extending the period during which the person can be found to have violated the conditions of supervised release.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether federal courts can apply a judicially-created 'fugitive tolling' doctrine to supervised release, effectively extending court-ordered conditions beyond the time specified in the judgment when a person absconds. The outcome affects revocation proceedings for thousands of individuals who abscond from supervised release each year.

positions.label: Supervised release is tolled during absconding
positions.summary: Holds that courts may apply a fugitive tolling doctrine to pause the running of supervised release when a supervisee absconds, extending the period during which violations can be found.

positions.label: Supervised release is not tolled
positions.summary: Holds that there is no judicial authority to toll supervised release terms without explicit statutory authorization, and the term continues to run even when a supervisee absconds.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2244(b)(1)'s bar on relitigating previously raised claims in habeas proceedings applies to federal prisoners filing motions under Section 2255.
splits.description: A longstanding 6-to-3 circuit split exists on whether federal prisoners face a stricter gatekeeping requirement when bringing successive collateral attacks on their convictions. If (b)(1) applies, federal prisoners are categorically barred from raising any claim they previously presented, in addition to the separate requirements in Section 2255(h). If it does not apply, prisoners need only satisfy 2255(h)'s requirements.

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) applies to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that the categorical bar on relitigating previously raised claims under § 2244(b)(1) applies to federal prisoners filing successive § 2255 motions, imposing an additional gatekeeping requirement.

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) does not apply to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that federal prisoners filing successive § 2255 motions need only satisfy § 2255(h)'s requirements of newly discovered evidence or a new rule of constitutional law, without the additional § 2244(b)(1) bar.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a candidate for federal office has Article III standing to challenge a state law that allows the counting of mail-in ballots received after Election Day.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether candidates can establish Article III standing to bring pre-election challenges to state election rules such as mail-in ballot counting deadlines. The resolution affects how easily candidates can challenge voting procedures nationwide before an election takes place.

positions.label: Candidates have standing
positions.summary: Holds that candidates for federal office have Article III standing to challenge state election laws that allegedly dilute or affect the counting of their votes, allowing pre-election challenges.

positions.label: Candidates lack standing
positions.summary: Holds that candidates do not have Article III standing to challenge election administration rules pre-election absent a more concrete and particularized injury.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

splits.legalQuestion: What legal standards govern claims of discrimination or unfair treatment in the operation of hospitality or business establishments?
splits.description: The circuits have applied differing standards to claims of discrimination in hospitality and business establishments, prompting SCOTUS review of the Second Circuit's approach. The decision could impact hospitality, retail, and other service industries nationwide by establishing or refining standards for fair treatment, discrimination liability, and damages.

positions.label: Broader liability standards
positions.summary: Applies a broader standard for establishing liability for discrimination or unfair treatment in business establishments, making it easier for plaintiffs to prevail.

positions.label: Narrower liability standards
positions.summary: Applies a narrower standard requiring a higher showing for claims of discrimination in business operations.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the rule of lenity takes precedence over agency or Sentencing Commission deference (Auer/Kisor deference) in the interpretation of ambiguous provisions that affect criminal sentences.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether courts should apply the rule of lenity or defer to agency/Commission interpretations when sentencing guidelines or criminal statutes are ambiguous. At least three circuits hold lenity trumps deference, while the Third Circuit has held that agency deference trumps lenity. Post-Loper Bright, this issue has gained additional significance.

positions.label: Lenity trumps deference
positions.summary: Holds that when a criminal sentencing provision is ambiguous, the rule of lenity applies and courts should not defer to agency or Commission interpretations that expand criminal liability.

positions.label: Deference trumps lenity
positions.summary: Holds that agency or Commission deference applies even in criminal sentencing contexts, and an anti-defendant reading of an ambiguous guideline can be upheld through deference rather than applying lenity.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Sentencing Guidelines' Application Note 1 to U.S.S.G. § 4B1.2, which adds inchoate offenses (conspiracy, aiding and abetting, attempt) to the definition of 'controlled substance offense,' is a valid and authoritative interpretation of the guideline text that does not mention inchoate offenses.
splits.description: Circuits are deeply split on whether Application Note 1 permissibly expands the definition of 'controlled substance offense' in the career-offender guideline to include conspiracy and other inchoate offenses, despite the guideline text's silence. Some circuits defer to the commentary under Stinson, while others hold it impermissibly expands the guideline's scope post-Kisor.

positions.label: Commentary is authoritative; inchoate offenses included
positions.summary: Holds that Application Note 1 is the Commission's authoritative interpretation of § 4B1.2(b) and properly includes inchoate offenses like conspiracy in the definition of 'controlled substance offense' for career-offender purposes.

positions.label: Commentary impermissibly expands guideline text; inchoate offenses excluded
positions.summary: Holds that the guideline text unambiguously excludes inchoate offenses by not mentioning them, so the commentary impermissibly expands the definition and is not entitled to deference under Kisor.

circuits.name: Sixth Circuit
circuits.caseName: United States v. Haynes (cited in split discussion)

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the word 'and' in the First Step Act's safety-valve provision, 18 U.S.C. § 3553(f)(1), is conjunctive (requiring all three criminal-history criteria to disqualify a defendant) or disjunctive (any one criterion is disqualifying).
splits.description: A deep circuit split exists on the meaning of 'and' in § 3553(f)(1). The Ninth and Eleventh Circuits hold that defendants are disqualified from safety-valve relief only if they meet all three criminal-history criteria, while the Fifth, Sixth, Seventh, and Eighth Circuits hold that possessing any one criterion is disqualifying. This split leads to dramatically different sentences for identically situated defendants depending on geography.

positions.label: 'And' is conjunctive — all three criteria required
positions.summary: Holds that the word 'and' in § 3553(f)(1) means all three criminal-history criteria must be satisfied to disqualify a defendant from safety-valve relief, so a defendant who meets only one or two criteria remains eligible.

positions.label: 'And' is disjunctive — any one criterion disqualifies
positions.summary: Holds that any one of the three criminal-history criteria in § 3553(f)(1) is independently disqualifying, effectively reading 'and' as 'or.'

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a state drug conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' under the Sentencing Guidelines when the state schedule covers substances not listed under the federal Controlled Substances Act.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether the career-offender guideline's definition of 'controlled substance offense' requires the underlying substance to be federally scheduled, or whether any state-law drug offense qualifies. The Eighth Circuit holds there is no federal-law limitation, while other circuits have required the substance to be federally controlled.

positions.label: No federal-law limitation — state offenses qualify broadly
positions.summary: Holds that U.S.S.G. § 4B1.2(b) broadly defines 'controlled substance offense' to include state law offenses even if the particular substance is not controlled under the federal Controlled Substances Act.

positions.label: Federal-law limitation applies — substance must be federally scheduled
positions.summary: Holds that a state drug conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' only if the underlying substance is also controlled under federal law, requiring a match between state and federal schedules.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a non-retroactive change in sentencing law (such as the First Step Act's anti-stacking amendment to 18 U.S.C. § 924(c)) can constitute an 'extraordinary and compelling reason' for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A), and whether the Sentencing Commission's policy statement permitting such consideration exceeds its statutory authority.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether non-retroactive changes in law can support compassionate release motions. The Seventh and Eighth Circuits have held that non-retroactive changes in law cannot contribute to extraordinary and compelling reasons for sentence reduction, while other circuits have permitted consideration of such changes. The Sentencing Commission's 2024 amendment to U.S.S.G. § 1B1.13(b)(6) attempted to authorize such consideration, but some circuits have found this exceeds the Commission's authority.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes cannot support compassionate release
positions.summary: Holds that a non-retroactive change in law, whether alone or combined with other factors, cannot constitute an 'extraordinary and compelling reason' for compassionate release, and the Commission's policy statement permitting otherwise exceeds its statutory authority.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes may support compassionate release
positions.summary: Holds that courts may consider non-retroactive changes in sentencing law as part of the analysis of extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release, consistent with the Sentencing Commission's policy statement.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether district courts may expressly impose punitive sanctions at supervised release revocation proceedings, or whether revocation sentences must be limited to non-punitive purposes.
splits.description: The Sixth Circuit permits district courts to expressly punish defendants for violations of supervised release, while other circuits hold that revocation sentences must serve non-punitive purposes such as promoting compliance and protecting the public. Dissenters in the Sixth Circuit have noted this places the circuit at the extreme of a circuit split.

positions.label: Punitive purpose is permissible
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may expressly punish defendants at supervised release revocation, allowing punitive considerations in revocation sentencing.

positions.label: Punitive purpose is impermissible
positions.summary: Holds that revocation sentences must be limited to non-punitive purposes such as promoting compliance with conditions and protecting the public, and courts may not impose punishment for the violation itself.

circuits.name: Third Circuit
circuits.caseName: (cited in Esteras dissent as contrary authority)

splits.legalQuestion: Whether post-petition, pre-conversion increases in the equity of a debtor's asset belong to the bankruptcy estate or to the debtor upon good-faith conversion from Chapter 13 to Chapter 7 under 11 U.S.C. § 348(f)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether property appreciation that occurs between a Chapter 13 filing and conversion to Chapter 7 belongs to the bankruptcy estate or the debtor. The Ninth Circuit holds that appreciation inures to the estate, while the dissent noted this creates a circuit split with circuits that hold such appreciation belongs to the debtor.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the estate
positions.summary: Holds that post-petition, pre-conversion increases in equity belong to the bankruptcy estate upon conversion, based on the broad scope of § 541(a)'s definition of 'property of the estate.'

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the debtor
positions.summary: Holds that the Bankruptcy Code's structure and § 348(f)(1)(A) establish that post-petition, pre-conversion appreciation belongs to the debtors, not the estate, to incentivize good-faith Chapter 13 participation.

circuits.name: Eighth Circuit
circuits.caseName: (cited in Castleman dissent as contrary authority)

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a federal prisoner challenging a BOP decision affecting the terms or conditions of confinement (such as denial of transfer to prerelease custody under the First Step Act) must proceed under habeas corpus or may bring a civil rights action.
splits.description: A longstanding circuit split exists on whether challenges to BOP conditions of confinement (as opposed to the fact or duration of confinement) must be brought exclusively through habeas corpus or may also be brought through civil rights actions like Bivens. The Eighth Circuit has acknowledged this 'unresolved conflict' spanning more than half a century, affecting federal prisoners' choice of remedy when challenging BOP decisions.

positions.label: Habeas is the exclusive remedy
positions.summary: Holds that challenges to BOP decisions affecting confinement conditions that implicate the fact or duration of imprisonment must be brought exclusively under habeas corpus statutes.

positions.label: Civil rights actions are also available
positions.summary: Holds that prisoners may challenge conditions of confinement through civil rights actions without being required to proceed exclusively through habeas corpus, particularly when they do not challenge the fact or duration of imprisonment itself.

circuits.name: Ninth Circuit
circuits.caseName: (cited in Fortner as contrary authority in longstanding split)

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a motion for attorney's fees under the Hyde Amendment is a civil matter subject to the civil appeal deadline, or a criminal matter subject to the criminal appeal deadline.
splits.description: Circuits have split on whether the Hyde Amendment, which permits criminal defendants to recover fees for defending against frivolous, vexatious, or bad-faith charges, creates a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case (subject to the 30-day civil appeal deadline) or is part of the criminal case (subject to the 14-day criminal appeal deadline). The Seventh Circuit joined the majority view that the civil deadline applies.

positions.label: Civil appeal deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment fee motion is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case, so the 30-day civil appeal deadline under Fed. R. App. P. 4(a) governs.

positions.label: Criminal appeal deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment fee motion is part of the criminal case and subject to the 14-day criminal appeal deadline under Fed. R. App. P. 4(b).

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a state law categorically barring transgender women from women's sports teams violates the Equal Protection Clause as applied to transgender women who have medically mitigated sex-based biological advantages, and whether as-applied equal protection challenges are viable under intermediate scrutiny.
splits.description: Circuits are divided on whether categorical bans on transgender athlete participation survive intermediate scrutiny when applied to individuals who have undergone medical transition. The case also raises the broader question of whether sex-based classifications affecting transgender individuals warrant heightened scrutiny.

positions.label: Categorical ban violates Equal Protection as applied
positions.summary: Holds that a categorical ban fails intermediate scrutiny as applied to transgender women who have medically mitigated biological advantages, because the state has not shown the ban is substantially related to its interest in competitive fairness for this subclass.

positions.label: Categorical ban does not violate Equal Protection
positions.summary: Holds that biological sex-based classifications in athletics are substantially related to the important governmental interest in fair competition and the safety of female athletes, even as applied to transgender women.

circuits.name: Fourth Circuit
circuits.caseName: B.P.J. v. West Virginia State Board of Education

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act (RLUIPA) clearly authorizes individual-capacity damages suits against state prison officials, and whether Congress has the constitutional power under the Spending Clause to impose such personal liability.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether RLUIPA's text provides sufficiently clear notice to authorize damages claims against prison officials in their individual capacities, implicating Spending Clause limits on Congress's ability to impose personal liability on individuals who are not direct recipients of federal funds.

positions.label: RLUIPA authorizes individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA's text and structure provide clear authorization for damages suits against state prison officials in their individual capacities.

positions.label: RLUIPA does not authorize individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA does not clearly authorize individual-capacity damages suits against prison officials, and the Spending Clause limits Congress's ability to impose such liability on non-recipients of federal funds.

circuits.name: Fifth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Sossamon v. Lone Star State of Texas

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Landor v. Louisiana Department of Corrections and Public Safety

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may consider factors related to potential errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as part of the 'extraordinary and compelling reasons' analysis for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether compassionate release motions may be used to raise claims that overlap with habeas corpus challenges, such as alleged sentencing errors or constitutional violations in the underlying conviction. Some circuits permit consideration of such factors, while others hold that § 3582(c)(1)(A) cannot be used as a substitute for § 2255 habeas relief.

positions.label: May consider conviction/sentence errors
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may consider legal errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as one factor in the extraordinary and compelling reasons analysis for compassionate release.

positions.label: Cannot use compassionate release for habeas-type claims
positions.summary: Holds that § 3582(c)(1)(A) is not an alternative avenue for claims properly raised under § 2255, and errors in conviction or sentencing cannot constitute extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Aviation Administration Authorization Act of 1994 (FAAAA) preempts state-law negligence claims against freight brokers who arrange transportation of property by motor carriers.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether the FAAAA's broad preemption clause, which prohibits states from enacting laws 'related to a price, route, or service of any... broker,' preempts common-law negligence claims against freight brokers for injuries arising from the carrier's operations. This split affects the liability exposure of freight brokers nationwide.

positions.label: FAAAA preempts broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are preempted by the FAAAA because they relate to the broker's services in arranging transportation.

circuits.name: Ninth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Miller v. C.H. Robinson Worldwide, Inc.

positions.label: FAAAA does not preempt broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are not preempted by the FAAAA because they are generally applicable common-law duties rather than regulations targeting broker services.

circuits.name: Eleventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act (FIFRA) preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims based on allegedly inadequate product labeling when the EPA has not required the specific warning.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether FIFRA's preemption provision bars state-law failure-to-warn claims against pesticide manufacturers when the claim is based on the absence of a warning that the EPA did not require. The split affects product liability litigation involving agricultural chemicals and consumer pesticide products.

positions.label: FIFRA preempts failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims that would effectively require labeling different from or in addition to what FIFRA and EPA regulations permit.

positions.label: FIFRA does not preempt failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA does not preempt state-law failure-to-warn claims because such claims impose requirements 'parallel to' rather than 'in addition to' FIFRA's labeling requirements.

circuits.name: Third Circuit
circuits.caseName: DeKalb Genetics Corp. v. Bayer CropScience

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Monsanto Company v. John L. Durnell

splits.legalQuestion: Whether 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3), which prohibits unlawful users of controlled substances from possessing firearms, violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users.
splits.description: Following the Supreme Court's decision in Bruen, circuits have split on whether § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by users of controlled substances — particularly marijuana — is constitutional. Some circuits have upheld the law under historical tradition analysis, while others have found it unconstitutional as applied to marijuana users.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is constitutional
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by unlawful drug users is consistent with the nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation and survives Second Amendment scrutiny.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is unconstitutional as applied
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3) violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users because the government has not demonstrated a historical tradition of disarming persons who use intoxicating substances.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether workers who distribute baked goods to retail stores qualify as 'transportation workers engaged in foreign or interstate commerce' under Section 1 of the Federal Arbitration Act, thereby exempting them from mandatory arbitration agreements.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on the scope of the FAA's Section 1 transportation worker exemption, specifically whether workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of a broader interstate distribution chain are 'transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce.' The split affects the enforceability of arbitration agreements for a broad class of last-mile delivery workers.

positions.label: Broad interpretation — last-mile workers exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of an interstate distribution chain are transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce exempt from the FAA.

positions.label: Narrow interpretation — last-mile workers not exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who merely distribute goods locally to retail stores are not transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce and remain subject to FAA arbitration agreements.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 47(b) of the Investment Company Act creates a private right of action allowing parties to a contract that violates the ICA to sue in federal court for rescission of that contract.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether § 47(b) of the ICA provides an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts made in violation of the Act. This affects the ability of private parties to enforce the ICA's protections against abusive investment company practices through direct federal court actions.

positions.label: Section 47(b) creates a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) creates an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts that violate the Investment Company Act, allowing private parties to sue directly.

circuits.name: Second Circuit
circuits.caseName: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

positions.label: Section 47(b) does not create a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) is a voidability provision rather than a private right of action, and only the SEC can enforce the ICA's prohibitions.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, as construed under the Gingles framework, can constitutionally compel race-based redistricting as a remedy for vote dilution, and whether compliance with Section 2 constitutes a compelling governmental interest justifying the use of race in drawing district lines.
splits.description: This case raises the question of whether race-conscious redistricting mandated by Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act is constitutionally permissible under the Equal Protection Clause. Lower courts have applied the Gingles framework to require consideration of race, but the constitutionality of this framework as applied is increasingly contested.

positions.label: Section 2 compels constitutionally permissible race-conscious redistricting
positions.summary: Holds that compliance with Section 2 of the VRA, as interpreted under the Gingles framework, constitutes a compelling interest that justifies the use of race in drawing district lines.

positions.label: Section 2's compelled race-based redistricting raises constitutional concerns
positions.summary: Holds or suggests that the Gingles framework's requirement of race-based redistricting may exceed constitutional limits under the Equal Protection Clause, particularly after Dobbs-era equal protection jurisprudence.

circuits.name: Eighth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Arkansas State Conference of the NAACP v. Arkansas Board of Apportionment
